passage: At 10:40 p.m. Afreen's phone lit up again: 'Guess I'll just sit alone on my birthday eve. Classic.' Chaitanya had sent six messages since Afreen said no to riding across Hyderabad for a late-night cake run; Afreen's exam was at nine the next morning. This was how it usually went. Skip a lecture to sit with Chaitanya after a fight at home. Lend the scooter again. Cancel on other friends because Chaitanya 'was having a terrible week'. Each yes bought a few calm days. Tonight Afreen sat on the bed in the rented room in Tolichowki, typing and deleting. Finally: 'Happy early birthday. I'm not coming tonight because of my exam. I'll take you for breakfast on Saturday.' The reply came fast: 'wow ok'. Afreen put the phone in a drawer and opened the revision notes.

qa.q: At what time was Afreen's exam the next morning?
qa.a: Afreen's exam was at nine the next morning.

qa.q: What might Afreen be feeling while typing and deleting?
qa.a: Afreen feels guilty and torn, used to buying calm days by saying yes, yet sure the exam matters.

'You picked them over me,' Joseph said, blocking the library stairs. 'After everything I did for you in first year.'
'I picked a project group, Joseph. Yours was full.'
'You could've asked me to make space. You didn't even think of me.'
'I did think of you. I asked on Monday, and you said you'd see.'
'Fine. I'll do everything alone. Like always.'
Uma felt the old pull to say sorry, to switch groups, to fix it. It had worked before; it always cost something.
'Joseph, I care about you. I'm staying in my group. And I'm happy to study with you on Thursday, like always.'
'So that's it?'
'That's what I can do. If you're upset, I'll listen. But I'm not switching.'
Joseph looked away, then muttered, 'Thursday, then.'

passage: Rafiq, you're asking what to do about your friend. Let your Rekha-aunty tell you about Shobha. We were twenty, sharing a room in a working women's hostel in Pune. Her fiancé phoned every hour and decided what she wore. One night I lost my temper: 'Either you leave him, or never talk to me about him again.' She never talked to me about him again. For four months she didn't talk to me at all. That silence frightened me more than he did. So I swallowed my pride and left a tiffin of her favourite poha outside her door with a note: 'No speeches. Just miss you.' She came back slowly. I listened, mostly. Once, only once, I told her what I saw. A year later she was the one who asked me to help her pack.

qa.a: Shobha likely felt judged and cornered, so she shut Rekha out rather than choose, and only later felt safe enough to ask for help.

passage: The offer letter from the Bengaluru design studio lay on the dining table of the Kandivali flat. Sahil's elder brother Sachin picked it up, read it and set it down very gently. 'I left college at nineteen to run Papa's hardware shop so you could study,' he said. 'And now you'll go a thousand kilometres away and leave me with all of it.' Sahil's chest tightened. Sachin had given up a lot; that was true. Last year Sahil had turned down an internship for the same reason and spent months quietly resentful. This time he sat down beside his brother. 'Bhaiya, I know what you gave up. I'm grateful every day. And I'm taking the job. I'll come home every Diwali, and we'll find help for the shop together.' Sachin didn't answer for a long time. Then he asked when the joining date was.

qa.a: The offer letter was from the Bengaluru design studio.

qa.a: Sahil felt guilty and torn, knowing the sacrifice was real, and remembering the resentment after giving in last year.

grounding: Shows a brother using his sacrifice to steer a career choice, and Sahil acknowledging that love while choosing for himself instead of complying and resenting.

passage:
'Delhi? For two whole years?' Avni Masi put down the ladle. 'I never married, Gurleen. I stayed in this house to raise you after your mother passed. And now you'll leave me with an empty kitchen.'
'Masi, please sit.'
'What is there to sit? Go, go. Who am I to stop you?'
'You're the person who packed my tiffin for fourteen years. I know that. I'm not forgetting it.'
'Then stay. Do the course here in Ludhiana.'
'The course I want isn't here, Masi. I've thought about it for months.'
Silence. The dal bubbled over.
'Who will I cook for?'
'Me, every holiday. And I'll call you every night at nine, and you'll tell me what you made.'
Avni Masi wiped her eyes with her dupatta. 'Nine sharp.'
'Nine sharp,' Gurleen said, and switched off the stove.

qa.a: Avni Masi wants Gurleen to do the course here in Ludhiana.

'Can I ask what the money is for?' The room went quiet. Varun's smile stayed, but his voice cooled: 'Doubt is how people drift.' Riding home through the rain, Gurpreet phoned his sister and told her everything, then muted the group chat for a week to think with a clear head.

passage: I'm Nazia, and last year I became a small copy of Yogesh without noticing. He was the final-year student who ran the college film society, and everything he said sounded right. I still think Yogesh is brilliant; the way he listens before he speaks is something I really did learn. passage: From the first week of the architecture course in Copenhagen, Emil made it clear he didn't like Mina. Mina felt the old urge to win him over, to bring cake, to be extra nice. She didn't. She moved her model to the window table and spent the afternoon on her roof design.

The answer was ugly and simple: Seema had failed that same entrance exam two years ago and never told anyone how much it hurt. That night she took out her old notes and looked up the next exam date.

passage: Hana had looked at Daniel's profile eleven times since breakfast. 'You look like you're about to bite someone.' Hana turned the phone face down and told her. Said aloud, it sounded less like hatred and more like grief for the summer she had lost. Lotte listened, then asked, 'So what are you going to play for the spring audition?' Hana muted Daniel's account and opened her score.

qa.a: Hana had looked at it eleven times since breakfast.

grounding: Shows someone fixated on a rival who asks what the dislike stands for, finds old hurt, and steps away from fuelling it.

passage: Thursday, 1 a.m. Zainab, just breathe. Writing this so I stop reading comments. Yesterday I posted a short video about why our college canteen should have a vegetarian counter and a halal counter side by side. By this evening it had been shared by strangers, and there are over four hundred comments. Some call me names I won't write here. Some say I should be thrown out of college. I typed three long replies and deleted every one. Pradeep came over with instant noodles and sat on the floor with me. He helped me screenshot the worst ones into a folder, then we turned off comments and blocked the accounts that tagged my college. 'These people don't know you,' he said. 'I do.' I'm still shaky. Tomorrow I'll send the folder to the student welfare office.
